findings.text: The opening tells a newcomer in plain words what Athena is and what sets it apart: one model does the work, another checks it, and the cost of each step is recorded. This part works.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This is Athena's own site, but the title, heading and almost all of the content are about firstmate, a different project. Someone who came to learn about Athena gets two sentences about it, then a long study of another tool.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title>; h1 "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The page says why the study matters, and the 44 claims link to exact file lines at a pinned commit, which backs that up. But the page never shows Athena's main job, turning a request into a code change, in action.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: The next steps can be found from a link at the top, but they are thin. There is no clone command and no list of prerequisites (for example a Rust toolchain or model API keys). The page also doesn't say where `athena ask` should be run or what it will produce.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: The page says "agent" always means firstmate's deciding AI and never a worker. Yet the relaunch lines (Start here, card t8, claim c19) call the stopped worker "the old agent", which breaks the page's own definition and will confuse a careful reader.
findings.source: "Firstmate's own deciding AI, called the agent on this page and never a worker" vs. "If a relaunch fails after the old agent was stopped, the prior durable record is restored and the report says no agent is running."

findings.text: Most of the page is dense internal detail: exit codes, a counter called places-held, and transition ids like t1 through t11. That is useful to someone checking how firstmate works, but too much for a first-time visitor who only wants the gist.
findings.source: Transitions cards t1–t11, e.g. t2 "Every worker place is held, so the spawn is deferred with exit 75 ... A spawn that cannot take the project lock, or cannot read the capacity declaration, exits 1 instead"

findings.text: Honest caveats like this one are repeated in several sections, and the opening term definitions are repeated in the Glossary. The repetition makes the page longer and harder to scan without adding anything.
findings.source: "in scope" entry: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it." (repeated in the Glossary and card t10)

findings.text: Being frank about limits is good. But for a newcomer, a note saying the first reading missed whole sections may undercut the main promise that Athena reads unfamiliar projects reliably, and the page does not say how those gaps were found and fixed.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths ... none was run, so no run confirmed that a script behaves as its header says."

findings.text: This section refers to a repository folder the newcomer has never seen and gives them nothing they can act on.
findings.source: About this page: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
